title: IndiGo and Air India Just Cut Up to 22 Percent of Domestic Flights. The Iran War Made Flying in India Unaffordable.
excerpt: Jet fuel prices have surged so high that India's two biggest carriers are pulling thousands of flights from their summer schedules. NRIs booking India travel will face fewer options and higher fares.
body:
India's two largest airlines have pulled the emergency brake on summer flying.

IndiGo, the country's dominant carrier with over 2,200 daily flights, has cut 7 to 10 percent of its planned domestic schedule for June and July. Air India has gone further — slashing 22 percent of domestic flights and trimming international routes by 250 weekly services. Together, the two airlines control roughly 90 percent of India's domestic air passenger market.

The reason is jet fuel. Aviation turbine fuel now accounts for up to 40 percent of airline operating costs, and the Iran war has sent crude oil prices on a sustained climb. Brent crude has swung between $89 and $107 per barrel in the past two weeks alone, with fresh U.S. strikes near the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday pushing prices back toward $96.

What Changed

Air India confirmed in a statement that it had "temporarily rationalised operations on certain domestic routes" between June and August, citing "the sustained impact of high fuel prices on overall operations." Passengers affected by cancellations will be offered alternative flights, complimentary date changes, or full refunds.

IndiGo has not commented publicly on the cuts. Industry sources say the airline is targeting unprofitable routes where load factors have dropped below breakeven thresholds.

The timing could not be worse. June and July are peak summer travel months, with millions of Indians flying domestically for holidays, weddings, and family visits. Fewer seats on the same routes means higher fares — exactly when demand is strongest.

The NRI Travel Squeeze

For the Indian diaspora, the cuts add another layer of friction to an already difficult travel season. Air India's international reductions — roughly 250 fewer weekly flights — have opened slots for foreign carriers to add India routes, but at premium pricing. The combination of expensive long-haul tickets, fewer domestic connections, and a weakened rupee (now at 95.68 to the dollar) is making India trips significantly more expensive than a year ago.

Several NRI travel forums have reported sharp fare increases on popular routes like Delhi-Goa, Mumbai-Kochi, and Bengaluru-Jaipur, with one-way tickets up 30 to 50 percent compared to the same period in 2025.

A Structural Problem

The cuts expose a vulnerability in India's aviation boom. The country has ordered hundreds of new aircraft from Boeing and Airbus, with deliveries stretching through the decade. But fleet expansion means little when fuel costs make every additional flight a potential loss-maker.

Air India, owned by the Tata Group and Singapore Airlines, recently posted a record annual loss of more than $2 billion — hammered not just by fuel costs but also by Pakistan's ban on Indian carriers in its airspace and a strong U.S. dollar.

The airline's losses underscore a broader industry reality: India's aviation market grew on the promise of cheap fares and expanding routes, but that model depends on affordable fuel. With the Strait of Hormuz still effectively closed and no clear timeline for reopening, airlines are managing costs the only way they can — by flying less.

IndiGo, while more profitable than Air India, faces the same math. The airline had already cut some long-haul flights before the war, citing operational constraints and airport congestion.

What Comes Next

If a U.S.-Iran deal reopens the Strait of Hormuz — a possibility that sent oil prices tumbling 5 percent on Wednesday before fresh strikes reversed the drop — fuel costs could stabilize. But airlines have already locked in summer schedules, and restoring cancelled flights takes weeks of operational planning.

For now, the message for anyone planning summer travel to or within India is straightforward: book early, expect to pay more, and build in flexibility. The days of last-minute ₹3,000 one-way domestic fares may not return until the geopolitics of oil do.
author: Diaspora Desk
